desc:
You are given the daily closing prices of a stock. The span of day i is the number of consecutive days ending at day i (including day i itself) for which the price was less than or equal to prices[i]. Equivalently, it is the distance back to the nearest earlier day with a strictly higher price (or to the start of the array if there is none).

Return the array of spans, one value per day.

Example: prices = [100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85] gives [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 4, 6]. On the last day the price 85 beats the five previous prices 75, 60, 70, 60, 80, but not 100.
hints: Walking back from every day until you hit a higher price is O(n<sup>2</sup>) for increasing prices.
The span of day i only depends on the nearest earlier day with a strictly higher price. Days with lower prices in between are 'hidden' behind day i for all later days too.
Keep a stack of indices with strictly decreasing prices. Pop while prices[top] ≤ prices[i]; then the span is i - top (or i + 1 if the stack is empty). Push i.
editorial: The span is the distance to the previous greater element. Process days left to right and keep a stack of day indices whose prices are strictly decreasing. For the new day i, all days on top with price ≤ prices[i] are absorbed into its span, so they are popped: for any future day they are either inside a longer span ending at i or beyond i, and in both cases day i is the better reference.

After popping, the top of the stack (if any) is the closest earlier day with a strictly higher price, so the span is i - top; with an empty stack it is i + 1. Every day is pushed and popped once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
